task.instructions:
Weekly water storage at two reservoirs, in thousand acre-feet (TAF), for weeks 1 through 26 of a refill season. Each list is in week order, week 1 first:
  Oroville: 1842.3, 1889.7, 1961.4, 2054.8, 2178.2, 2310.6, 2402.9, 2551.3, 2698.7, 2814.1, 2946.5, 3057.8, 3188.2, 3271.6, 3346.9, 3421.4, 3452.7, 3418.5, 3352.1, 3260.4, 3147.8, 3021.6, 2896.3, 2758.9, 2617.2, 2483.5
  Shasta:   2214.6, 2263.1, 2331.8, 2408.5, 2496.2, 2571.9, 2648.3, 2724.7, 2801.4, 2877.8, 2943.2, 3008.6, 3062.9, 3104.3, 3138.7, 3159.2, 3171.5, 3168.4, 3142.7, 3098.1, 3041.6, 2974.2, 2899.5, 2818.3, 2731.6, 2640.9
Using matplotlib, draw both series as lines on one set of axes, with the week number (1..26) on the x axis and storage on the y axis.
Requirements:
- Label the two lines exactly `Oroville` and `Shasta`, and show a legend.
- Find the highest storage value reached by the OROVILLE series and the week it occurs in. Do not hard-code a guess; read it off the data.
- Mark that single peak point with a distinct marker drawn on top of the line (for example a call to `ax.scatter`, or a one-point `ax.plot`), so it stands out from the rest of the curve.
- Add a text annotation next to the peak reading exactly `Peak: <value> TAF (week <n>)`, substituting the peak value in TAF (with its one decimal place, no thousands separator) and the week number. For instance if the peak were 1234.5 TAF in week 3 the label would read `Peak: 1234.5 TAF (week 3)`.
- The y axis must start at 0.
- Give the chart a title and label both axes.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Data for Oroville and Shasta reservoirs
oroville_data = [
    1842.3, 1889.7, 1961.4, 2054.8, 2178.2, 2310.6, 2402.9, 2551.3, 
    2698.7, 2814.1, 2946.5, 3057.8, 3188.2, 3271.6, 3346.9, 3421.4, 
    3452.7, 3418.5, 3352.1, 3260.4, 3147.8, 3021.6, 2896.3, 2758.9,

]

    2214.6, 2263.1, 2331.8, 2408.5, 2496.2, 2571.9, 2648.3, 2724.7, 
    2801.4, 2877.8, 2943.2, 3008.6, 3062.9, 3104.3, 3138.7, 3159.2, 
    3171.5, 3168.4, 3142.7, 3098.1, 3041.6, 2974.2, 2899.5, 2818.3, 
    2731.6, 2640.9
]

# Week numbers (1 to 26)
weeks = list(range(1, 27))

# Create the plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Plot Oroville data
oroville_line, = ax.plot(weeks, oroville_data, label='Oroville')

# Plot Shasta data
shasta_line, = ax.plot(weeks, shasta_data, label='Shasta')

# Find the peak value and its week for Oroville
peak_value = max(oroville_data)
peak_week = oroville_data.index(peak_value) + 1  # +1 because weeks start at 1

# Mark the peak point
ax.scatter(peak_week, peak_value, color='red', zorder=5, label='Peak')

# Add annotation for the peak
peak_annotation = f"Peak: {peak_value:.1f} TAF (week {peak_week})"
ax.annotate(peak_annotation, xy=(peak_week, peak_value), xytext=(peak_week + 1, peak_value + 50),
            arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', shrink=0.05), fontsize=9)

# Set y-axis to start at 0

# Add labels and title
